lessons.title: Reflection and curved mirrors
lessons.programRef: Form 4 Physics — Reflection, curved mirrors, refraction and lenses (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use the laws of reflection and describe the image in a plane mirror.
Describe the action of concave and convex mirrors on parallel rays.
Use the mirror formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v and magnification.
reviewNotes: Real-is-positive sign convention used; check whether the syllabus uses the Cartesian or the real-is-positive convention.
The ray diagram is schematic (paraxial rays).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Laws of reflection
blocks.md:
1. The angle of incidence **i** equals the angle of reflection **r** (both measured from the normal).
2. The incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.

A **plane mirror** forms a **virtual**, upright image, the same size as the object and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. A **virtual** image cannot be shown on a screen; a **real** image can. If a plane mirror turns by θ, the reflected ray turns by 2θ.

blocks.title: Curved mirrors
blocks.md: A **concave** (converging) mirror brings parallel rays to the **principal focus F**. The distance from the mirror to F is the **focal length f**; the **centre of curvature C** is at 2f. A **convex** (diverging) mirror spreads parallel rays out as if from a virtual focus behind it. Rays: parallel to the axis → through F; through F → parallel to the axis; through C → back along itself.

blocks.caption: Image in a concave mirror when the object is beyond C: real, inverted and smaller.
blocks.alt: A concave mirror on the right, an object arrow beyond C on the left and a smaller inverted image arrow between C and F, with two reflected rays meeting at the image tip.

blocks.title: Mirror formula and uses
blocks.md: **1/f = 1/u + 1/v** (real-is-positive: u object distance, v image distance, f focal length of a concave mirror positive). **Magnification m = v / u = image height ÷ object height**. Uses: **concave**: torch and headlight reflectors, shaving mirrors, dentists' mirrors (magnified when the object is within f); **convex**: driving mirrors and shop security mirrors because they give a wide field of view.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Measure angles from the **normal**, not from the mirror.
- The image in a plane mirror is as far **behind** the mirror as the object is in front, so the distance between object and image is twice the distance to the mirror.
- A real image is inverted; a virtual image formed by a mirror is upright.

blocks.title: Image in a concave mirror
blocks.statement: An object is 30 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and the magnification.
steps: m = v ÷ u = 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5 (half the size, real, inverted).

blocks.title: Plane mirror distance
blocks.statement: A boy stands 2.5 m from a plane mirror and walks 1 m towards it. How far is he now from his image?
steps: He is now 2.5 − 1 = 1.5 m from the mirror.
The image is 1.5 m behind it: distance = 3.0 m.

lessons.title: Refraction and lenses
lessons.programRef: Form 4 Physics — Reflection, curved mirrors, refraction and lenses (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe refraction and use the refractive index n = sin i / sin r.
Explain total internal reflection and the critical angle.
Describe image formation by a converging lens and use 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.
reviewNotes: n for water 1.33 and glass 1.5 are standard school values; the critical angle for water is 48.8°, quoted as about 49°.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Refraction
blocks.md: **Refraction** is the bending of light when it passes from one transparent material to another, because its **speed changes**. Light entering a **denser** medium (air to glass) bends **towards the normal**; leaving it bends **away**. The **refractive index** **n = sin i ÷ sin r** (i in air, r in the material); n = 1.33 for water and about 1.5 for glass. Refraction makes a pool look shallower than it is.

blocks.caption: A ray passing from air into glass bends towards the normal.
blocks.alt: A ray hitting the top of a glass block at 45 degrees to the normal and bending to about 28 degrees inside the glass.

blocks.title: Total internal reflection
blocks.md: When light travels from a **denser to a less dense** medium and the angle of incidence is **larger than the critical angle c**, **all** the light is reflected inside: **total internal reflection**. **sin c = 1 / n**. For glass c ≈ 42°; for water c ≈ 49°. Uses: prisms in binoculars, bicycle reflectors, **optical fibres** for telephone and internet signals and for medical viewing.

blocks.caption: Image formed by a converging lens when the object is beyond 2F: real, inverted and smaller.
blocks.alt: A converging lens with an object arrow far to the left and a smaller inverted image arrow on the right, with two rays crossing at the image tip.

blocks.title: Converging lens
blocks.md: A **converging (convex) lens** brings parallel rays to the **principal focus F**. **1/f = 1/u + 1/v** (real-is-positive), **m = v / u**. Object beyond 2F: small real inverted image (camera). Object between F and 2F: enlarged real image (projector). Object **inside F**: enlarged, upright, **virtual** image: a **magnifying glass**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- n = sin i ÷ sin r uses the sines of angles, not the angles themselves.
- Total internal reflection needs **both** a denser-to-less-dense path **and** an angle above c.
- A magnifying glass uses the object **inside** the focal length.
